utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I take it that the Defence is ready to conclude the cross-examination. As indicated yesterday, the time limit is seven minutes. Madam usher, could you please...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst the witness is being brought in, a brief point of clarification in relation to the 92 bis ruling: The names not mentioned, are they not admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For various reasons, not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, General. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic. Could it be redacted, please, Madam Registrar. This is now the third time on the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to ask for a closed session in order to ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will turn into closed session at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General, could you confirm to us that in your talks with General Galic about the crossing of soldiers across the airport runway, did you receive any guidance as to this problem should be addressed at a higher level, it should be discussed at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the only person dealing with this issue. General Morillon, the commander of the Bosnian UN troops, he was in charge of the issue, and the Zagreb party was also aware of this. I told them that -- I told the Serb party that their attacks affected the French Battalion. Galic was very clear. He said, "If you wanted to stop the fire, you should stop the movement around the airport from the other side." I have talked to the other side and I asked Mr. Ganic from the other party to take drastic measures in order to prevent the flow of civilians through the airport. What we meant was the civilians, civilians, old people, women, children. Those people are civilian and not soldiers. So the subject was clear to me. The attitude of Mr. Galic was clear. The UN commander in Yugoslavia in Bosnia was fully aware of this issue. This subject was contained in the reports exchanged between the various units, and when I put the issue to Mr. Galic, I wasn't alone. I used to be accompanied by my deputy and the staff members who used to accompany me in this sort of negotiations. And I do hope that you have received the necessary clarification now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, at the time when you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, it was quite clear how much time you would have. Your time is over now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing arising, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I have only one question, General. Yesterday, you said that the report on civilian casualties came from the mass media and from official quarters. Well, in fact I will make two questions. The first one is: What do you mean by "official quarters"?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to receive numerous reports from all sides. Each side claims that they suffered from casualties and losses, and the same applies to the other side. So we used to receive official documents. I do have some specimen of these documents we used to receive then. Those reports depict the losses and the casualties in the various sectors in Bosnia. Those reports depict the casualties as a consequence of the attacks. Those are routine reports reaching us from official quarters relating to the losses and casualties and so on and so forth. In addition to that, we used to monitor everything. We used to monitor the press releases and the press coverage and extract what is of interest to us. Obviously, we did not take this material only as far as it concerns us in our daily business. We used to notice that the information coming from our own sources, namely, the observers, those reports put it clearly that the bombing of the Serbs was more intensive than the bombing coming out of the Bosnian side outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: What I would like to know is whether the UN checked or used to check whether those reports and the reports of the mass media were reliable, were accurate, or not?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can tell you, under those circumstances, it was difficult, quite impossible, to substantiate anything or to be sure 100 per cent about the responsible party or who has done that. Obviously, the police has carried out investigations in addition to other coverage made by the observers. However, we did focus on the incidents within the UN area. We Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were not taking part in the investigation activities. We did not have the adequate mechanism within the UN to follow this line of activities. The investigation, first who did open fire, for example, we did not have this activity listed in order to investigate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: General, when you mentioned the police, was it the UN police or the BH police?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police -- the police work is related generally to the discipline matters. For example, like the incident I referred to the effect that the car was stolen and the accused or the accused persons were part of the Ukrainian Battalion, and we did enquire into this matter and we took the necessary measures then. In addition to that, the police used to accompany the UNHCR and the Red Cross representatives in their daily work and the police used to take part in preparing the reports concerning some illegal activities. There is also a channel of command between the Sarajevo command and higher hierarchy in order to let the flow of reports go smoothly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like you to clarify two points. The first one is in relation to what you had said about the headquarters. So you said that the headquarters of an officer who was called Mustafa, if I remember correctly, was on the first floor of a building. Did this -- was this building also -- were there also civilians in this building or was it only used as headquarters?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to meet with Mustafa in a separate building, but he had his own command and he had his own bodyguards from the Bosnian forces. And I used to meet with him in his office, and the impression I got was that the office was purely military and there were no signs of any civilians in the office. But in the surroundings, there were houses, there were civilian areas. But the building itself was occupied by military troops. There were other times where I met with him in -- with Colonel Siber in another building, but the building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't know of headquarters which was located in a building that also included civilians or in a building where civilians also lived?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of what was happening in other HQs, but within Sarajevo these are the two buildings that I was concerned with. I used to have my meetings in three places: The Presidency, with the political and military staff, and another meeting at HQ Sarajevo with Mustafa and Colonel Siber, Chief of Staff of the Bosnian forces. These are the three buildings where I had my meetings. Of course, the Presidency is known to everybody, but the two other buildings where I had my meetings were occupied by military troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have knowledge of an agreement that the headquarters of both sides are not targeted or should not be targeted?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that was one of the most confusing aspects that I witnessed during my tenure there. There were some buildings that were never touched or grazed by any bullets. However, it came to my knowledge that there were rounds landing in the proximity of these buildings. Apart from the Presidency, none of these buildings were touched by shrapnel or one -- during a visit by Mr. Boutros-Ghali, we were showing him where the rounds were fired. The buildings, the HQs which were military, were not affected by the shelling. There were signs of certain marks, but nothing major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We spoke of a strategy in a sense that the Presidency would have been targeted by the Bosniak side, by themselves, in order to attract the attention of the international community for propaganda purposes. Since you mentioned the visit of the Secretary-General of the United Nations, so there is -- there are some rumours that what -- when there was firing at the Presidency, that there was some manipulations and that the firing was not coming from the Serb side. Were you aware of these rumours, at least?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I saw the marks of the shelling before the arrival of the Secretary-General of the UN. I saw them myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My very last question: You said that the Bosniak side had mortars of middle and small calibres and they did not have large-calibre mortars. What do you mean by "middle calibre," "medium calibre"? To how many millimetres would medium calibre go to?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well established that small calibre, 60 millimetres; medium calibre, 88 millimetres; and higher go from 120 to 160.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 120 millimetres is large calibre?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The higher calibres operate from fixed bases. They might have had high calibre mortars. I was not in a position to visit the engagement points or confrontation lines, but the calibre use depends on the mobility the forces require. And a higher calibre requires a more sophisticated measure of launching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General, I have one question for you. You just answered a question of Judge El Mahdi by saying that you saw the marks of the shelling before the arrival of the Secretary-General of the UN. The question was about BiH weapons firing at their own positions. And when you say you saw the marks of the shelling, could you tell us how and whether and how you could identify whether these were marks from Serbian shelling or from BiH shelling?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not specify which party was responsible for the shelling. I just saw marks of the shelling on the building. It is difficult to determine the source of the shelling from these marks. Of course, the Bosnian side always claimed or alleged that these marks were caused by Serbian shelling. And of course, both sides always denied responsibility and blamed the shelling on the other side. And that has always been one of the main problems that we tried to settle. There was a war of words, a war of allegations, more than a war of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This perfectly clarifies your answer. I think I now understand your answer better. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Defence just had an observation to make in the same sense, in relation to the answer given by the General, just to find out whether the police that he was talking about, whether that was BH police or UN police. He answered "yes" to this question, but I think that a clarification would be necessary because we don't know really -- we could perhaps conclude, but I don't think it appears very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it is Ms. Pilipovic who deals with the examination of this witness, as I told you before. I also told you that tandem operation at this moment was not allowed in this sense. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In this case, I am very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: General, when you spoke of the police, you said "yes," that was your answer, and then you explained what I understood as the functions of the UN police. So when you said -- when you mentioned investigations made by the police, you were referring to the BH police, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in the structure of the command there are the troops, there are the observers, and there is a UN Military Police. When I speak about the police, that is the police force within my command that investigates reports, coordinates with humanitarian agencies, and all these people are under my command. They investigate issues relating to work concerning the UN. What happens with the Bosnian police is none of my concern. I used to confront the Bosnian police in cases where they prevented movement of UN personnel into the compound, outside the compound. And I remember I had a confrontation with one -- with a person called Abdul Habib and another police commander, and I threatened them to bring the whole issue into the open and tell the whole world that their forces have been trying to hamper the movements of UN personnel. The only time where we had contact with them is when they sent us a report about a stolen vehicle and I initiated an inquiry within my structure about this stolen vehicle, and otherwise I had no contact with these forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: When you mentioned the police investigations, were you referring to the BH police; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HUSSEIN ALI ABDEL-RAZEK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was talking about the police force of the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General, this concludes your testimony in this Court. It is important for the Chamber to hear the evidence, to hear the answers put to you by both parties and by the Chamber itself. I thank you very much for coming and testifying in this Court. And I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask if Ms. Pilipovic could be dealing with anything so that I can go and get the witness, our expert who is waiting in the lawyers' chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Mr. Ierace, I take it that Mr. Philipps is ready to continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As far as I know. It may take him a minute or two, I should think, to set up the computer. Would a short adjournment of five minutes be appropriate or so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, perhaps when he is doing so, I perhaps should add something to what I said yesterday to you when you asked whether you would get more time. I then did not have yet your letter of the 15th of July which was, I take it, distributed to the Defence and not to the Chamber. So I didn't know that. What we see, as a matter of fact, on your schedule, as you indicated already in the letter yourself, that you stretched more or less the time for each of the witnesses, and having gone through what we can expect the Prosecution will do, time can be gained considerably on the presentation of the evidence in chief of the expert witnesses. When the expert witnesses appear, we have read the reports in detail. So there is no need -- we had the experience, I think last week or the week before with Mr. Stamp, who took, for example, 45 minutes correcting minor adjustments in the expert witness report. You may take it that the Chamber knows the content of the report. So a very short introduction or perhaps a highlighting of a few items that could be better understood by a further explanation will do. But, otherwise, we should proceed as soon as possible to the cross-examination. And of course, if then certain issues might turn out to be very unclear, then, of course, there will be granted a bit more time in re-examination in order to clarify them. The Chamber is concerned about to hear what it has read already extensively. That is my first observation. The second observation is the Chamber indicated to the Prosecution that it might be wise to prepare for filling in a lot of time as far as the expert takes and Hinchliffe were concerned. The scheduling, as we see it now, leaves no room for that. I mean, Mr. Hinchliffe is just at the end of your list, so there is nothing to fill in any more. The same is not perhaps true for Mr. Higgs, but I would say that on the total of seven days, approximately, that has been scheduled for the expert witnesses, there might be three days you could save on that. I am just indicating since I only -- since I felt yesterday that you felt that it was difficult to find those times, to give you just some guidance as where the Chamber would seek to gain that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, two matters: First a general observation and then a specific question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The general observation is that the Prosecution is in an extremely difficult position. We will do our best. And in due course, I will update you. Some of the issues which contribute to our difficulties are that it takes time to organise witnesses to travel to The Hague, and I really have no confidence in our ability to stick to a timetable. And I say that with the qualification that a number of various matters contribute to that. And again, the last witness is a prime Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. example. One hour and 20 minutes in chief and he finishes an hour into the second day, for a number of reasons. I do emphasise that, for a number of reasons. Mr. President, in relation to the specific query, tomorrow we call General Karavelic. One of the matters that I will deal with through him, various maps which relate to the scheduled sniping and shelling incidents. Rather than have him correct the confrontation line positions on those maps, it would save, I think, considerable time if he did that this afternoon and then, during his testimony, explain what he had done and why he had done it. So, Mr. President, I would be grateful if in due course you could give us some guidance in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will let you know, I think, after the first break. Madam Usher, can you please escort Mr. Philipps into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again while we are waiting on Mr. Philipps, I should say something about Mr. Hinchliffe. I assure you that there was no other place we could place -- no other position in the timetable for us to place Mr. Hinchliffe. I was very mindful of what you said to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Given his unavailability for any time other than the last week, the alternative was to move (redacted), and a lot of negotiations and preparation had gone into organising those two days for (redacted).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an estimate on how much time you would still need with Mr. Philipps in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am hopeful I can do it in an hour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the technicians need a little bit more time for the set up. Is there any reason why it is different now from what it was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the technician still needs some time, perhaps we could do, at the same time, some other things. I asked the Defence to give some clarification by the beginning of this week of the time, the number of witnesses and the time they think they would need to present the Defence case. Could you give us a global idea of that, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence is working on a concept which it would present to the Chamber. In view of the problem with the arrival of the witnesses, we are still not able at the moment to give the Chamber definite information about a schedule, how many witnesses the Defence would be able to call in presenting their case. I expect that we will be able to provide the Chamber with a provisional schedule by Friday. I wanted also to say to the Chamber that the Defence expert who wanted to be present during the examination of Mr. Hinchliffe, which has been changed to the 2nd of August 2002, will be able to be in The Hague during those two days. The only problem we had is the problem with the visa, which he hasn't received that - but we expect this problem to be resolved - even though the request for the visa was submitted on the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are any problems remaining as far as the visa is concerned, inform the Chamber so that we can, if necessary, intervene. But let's first give it the ordinary course. But Ms. Pilipovic, I would like you -- I mean, I do understand that the Defence is not able yet to give a definite list and a definite schedule, but what do you have approximately in mind. Are we talking about 40 witnesses, 80 witnesses, 180 witnesses? That is what I asked the Defence to do, is to give us an impression of what we could expect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence at this point, and this is not official, expects to have about 100 witnesses on its list. But, like I said, the problem is that we are here in The Hague all of the time, so we are not able to get in touch with our investigators and the expert advisors. So that we are not able at this point to inform the Chamber about a schedule, particularly when we are speaking about witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are talking about 100 witnesses, let's just take it as a starting point. I am not expressing any view of the Chamber on whether that would be acceptable or not. But how much time did you have in mind, the presentation of the Defence case would then take, two months, five months, one year and-a-half?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we remained with this number of witnesses I mentioned, it might vary. It might be a smaller number of witnesses, depending on your decision. At this point, we estimate that we would need a minimum of three months. But, as I say, this is a rough estimate and this is why I wanted to think about it again by the end of the week -- think about it until the end of the week and then be able to present the Chamber with a definite list of witnesses as well as a time estimate of how much time we would need. But at the moment, our problem is with the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that we need -- we have to leave the courtroom anyhow. But let me just put the last question to you, Ms. Pilipovic. When you are talking about three months, would that include the cross-examination by the Prosecution or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I was just talking about the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Let me just confer for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we will have the break, I would like to turn into closed session just for one second, to deal with another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, can you please escort Mr. Philipps into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Philipps. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Philipps. I think on the last occasion, we got as far as slide number 45. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is 44 or 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you go back to slide 44, if you can. As we proceed from this point, I think now that you have explained most of the symbols and the manner in which you have structured the chart, we should be able to increase the pace, and perhaps you can draw our attention to only matters that are of a different type to what you have already explained. So in that regard, with that in mind, could you please explain this slide?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This slide shows the brigade headquarters of the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, which replaced or took the place of the Vogosca Brigade, and consequently the Vogosca operational group no longer existed, as this brigade took on all of the brigades that had previously been part Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the Vogosca operational group, with the exception of the Ilijas Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I take it from the information on the slide that it occurred by March 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between October 1993 and March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next slide shows three of the battalions that formed part of the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade. On the left we can see a battalion which previously was the Rajlovac Brigade; in the centre, a battalion of the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade; and on the right, the Kosevo or Radava Brigade, which became the 5th battalion of the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the chart, are those developments indicated by a broken red line with arrowheads?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the main chart, that is correct. A red line indicates the actual change of those brigade positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please point to that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next slide shows three more battalions of the Sarajevo -- the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The next slide being number 46, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could you please include the number of the slide as you go to each new one? Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next slide, which is number 47, shows the logistics battalion of the 3rd Brigade, which was there to support that brigade with supplies, transport, et cetera. The next slide, which is slide number 48, returns to the main chart. You will have noticed that no artillery was shown in the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade. In fact, it did have artillery. All its artillery came from what was previously the Vogosca Brigade. So I have not repeated all the artillery that I have previously shown under the Vogosca Brigade. Slide number 48 shows the position of the Kosevo Brigade which, as we have already seen, between October 1993 and March 1994, became part of the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade. Up until October 1993, the brigade consisted of the following. This is slide number 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just before you move on to that. On the main chart, above and beneath the red dotted arrow that we referred to previously showing the development of the Kosevo Light Infantry Brigade into part of the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, you have the words "moved and downsized by January 1994." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slide number 49 shows the headquarters of the Kosevo Brigade. This brigade is an example of one of those brigades I have mentioned earlier which was slightly smaller than the other brigades. Indeed, it was really only the size of perhaps a reinforced battalion. We can see in this slide of note that the commander of the brigade, Momcilo Krajisnik, his rank was actually only sergeant. Slide number 50 shows two units within the Kosevo Brigade: one unidentified unit, which probably became the Radava or was the Radava Battalion, and was an attached artillery unit. Slide number 51 returns to the main chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Incidentally, while you are on the main chart, in terms of the universal structure of a corps, is there sometimes another level of organisation between the brigades and the corps headquarters? Or is it typically a brigade and then the corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some armies, a corps can be divided into divisions which consist of a number of brigades. In the case of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the corps is divided up simply into brigades, and for part of that time had an operational group which covered a few of those brigades as discussed. So in the case, in fact, of the VRS in general, and specifically the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, there are no divisions, only brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This slide number 51 indicates the position of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before you go to the next slide, you told us, I think on the first day that you gave evidence, that you have placed the various brigades on the chart in the order in which they operated around Sarajevo, I think you said in a clockwise direction. Going back to the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, could you tell us in approximate terms whereabouts they were placed geographically around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade took over the positions of the Rajlovac Brigade which was positioned in Rajlovac. The Vogosca Brigade, which was in Vogosca, and the Kosevo brigade, which was in the Kosevo area, all of those being in a clockwise direction to the north of Sarajevo. This means that the 3rd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, when it was formed, was formed in a position that made it next to the 1st Romania Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And whereabouts was that geographically?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Romania Infantry Brigade covered the area from the edge of Kosevo in a direction all the way around the outside of Sarajevo to the borders of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In other words, does that mean extending from the north-east to the east, to the south-east and to the south?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And also facing outward from Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say "facing outward," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also a front for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps which was outside Sarajevo, that is, the brigades themselves were not always simply facing inwards to Sarajevo but were also facing outwards to the ABiH around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have heard evidence in the trial about Mount Trebevic. Was Mount Trebevic within the territorial control of the 1st Romania Infantry Brigade, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly have evidence or have information to show that parts of the 1st Romania Infantry Brigade held parts of Trebevic. But I would be hard pressed to draw an exact line as to the boundary between the 1st Romania Infantry Brigade and the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will draw to your attention two other places. If you know which brigade they were in in terms of territory, please indicate. The first is Poljine.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to consult a map to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spicasta Stijena, at one time, may have been within the boundary of the Kosevo Brigade and later may have been within the boundary of the 1st Romania Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an area just to the north of Sedrenik in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This slide, number 52, shows the brigade headquarters of the 1st Romania Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just before you leave that slide, Dragomir Milosevic appears on it as the brigade commander between September and January 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is shown as the brigade commander for those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You gave evidence that he was the deputy corps commander, I think, at a later point. Did he go directly from this position to that position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check whether he went directly from this position to become the Chief of Staff. I would have the check the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Milosevic here shown did not strictly hand over directly to the new brigade commander, Colonel Vlado Lizdek. There was not a direct handover between the two, Dragomir Milosevic having left that post before Colonel Vlado Lizdek arrived, and hence the dotted line with the word "gap" between the two. The only other fact worth noting about the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, like many of the other large-sized brigades or normal-sized brigades, [Realtime transcript read in error "sized brigades or large brigades"] it attempted to form the headquarters which matched the staff positions of the corps headquarters. Slide number 53 shows the infantry battalions within the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could just ask you to pause there for a moment. I take you back to the last observation you made on the previous slide. The only other fact worth noting, the 1st Infantry Brigade, like any other sized brigades or large brigades, attempted to form the headquarters which matched staff positions of the corps headquarters. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade headquarters would have a staff which dealt with the staff of the corps headquarters. And so where it was possible, the brigade commander would attempt to have an operations staff officer to match the operations department in the corps headquarters so that information could be passed from one to another, simply, and also replicate the three other staff positions, that is, either with logistics or each of those staff positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You referred to the territory occupied by that brigade, and it might be thought that that was a relatively large territory or certainly a considerable length of the confrontation line around Sarajevo. Is that relevant to the characteristic you observed about the structure of the brigade? Is there any connection, do you think?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The length of the front of this particular brigade relates to the type of ground that the brigade was holding. Most of the ground that 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade held was in open country or mountainous areas, and many fewer troops are required to hold a longer length of front in such an area. So, for example, a battalion might be able to hold several kilometres of ground in an open area, whereas in an urban environment it can only hold a very narrow front.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way: Are you aware of any reason as to why that brigade had an attempted replication of the corps command structure?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was an attempt of all brigades to match the staff within the corps so that they could communicate easily with the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next slide is number 54 and shows the supporting arms for the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, that is, first of all, two artillery batteries, one consisting of 76-millimetre mountain guns and the other an anti-aircraft battery of 20-millimetre cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: By way of explanation of the diagram on the screen, do you mean to indicate that you found one reference to four mountain guns, 76 millimetre, and a reference to three 20-millimetre anti-aircraft cannons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In this case, the information came directly from the brigade commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in a general sense in relation to armaments indicated on the chart, do you say that this was the entirety of the armaments or rather that you simply indicate the armaments of which you have some awareness of their existence through documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, I am not sure whether there are more artillery pieces attached to the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, but I do know that on certain occasions, artillery was temporarily attached from the corps, that is, from the mixed artillery regiment belonging to the corps. There may be other artillery units within the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, but I do not have information on them, if they do exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next slide is number 55 and shows the other supporting arms for the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade, such as military police, engineers, logistics. The only interesting fact here is that on the 25th of May, 1993, part of the organisation of the Ministry of Interior, the MUP, was temporarily attached to the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. It seems quite -- this is the only occasion where I have seen Ministry of Interior troops being temporarily attached, not normally forming part, of course, of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Slide number 56 returns to the main chart and shows the position of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Slide number 57 shows the brigade headquarters of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. This brigade was again a normal-sized brigade, that is, a relatively full strength brigade in comparison to the Rajlovac, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kosevo or 2nd Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Where was its location, geographically?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade held a position from Grbavica around to the south of Sarajevo as far as Lukavica and slightly south of Lukavica. Slight number 58 shows what was the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. This battalion was detached at some period - I am not sure when - from the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade to the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. It was the case that the brigade commander had felt that his front was too large and he could not hold Grbavica as well as the other parts of his front. And so the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade was resubordinated to the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Slide number 59 shows two more battalions of the Sarajevo 1st Mechanised Brigade, an armoured battalion and an infantry battalion called the Kasindol Battalion. The armoured battalion that is of note is equipped with a number of T-55 tanks and also the M-80 mechanised infantry combat vehicle. Slide number 60 continues to show three more battalions, part of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade and a sniper platoon attached to the brigade. It is worth noting that the mechanised battalion on the top left may not have been part of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, as I only have the formation order of that battalion and no information as to its existence or use after that date. Slide number 61 shows the supporting arms for the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, specifically, a mixed artillery battalion consisting of 155-millimetre Howitzers and 120-millimetre mortars, and also a self-propelled light anti-aircraft battalion consisting of anti-aircraft cannons of varying size, mostly mounted on trucks or similar vehicles. Slide number 62 continues with the brigade supporting arms of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, a logistics battalion, a military police company, an engineer unit, and a communications company. Slide number 63 returns to the main diagram and this time shows the corps supporting arms, that is, all the units directly subordinated to the corps headquarters that were there to support the work of the corps and of the brigades. Starting from the left, first of all, the slide shows the 4th Mixed Anti-tank Artillery Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. On the chart, these units, these regiments and so on, appear at the bottom, which might suggest at first glance that the relative significance of them was less than, not only the brigades but also the battalions, even the companies and the platoons. If you had an unrestricted chart in terms of area, where would they go in terms of indicating their significance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two points arise here: One is that they are subordinate to the corps headquarters in the same way that brigades are subordinate to the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you mean by that immediately subordinate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The corps headquarters and the corps command would give direct orders to these units, in the same way -- or to the commanders of these units, in the same way that the corps command would give direct orders to brigade headquarters and to brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, looking ahead a little, it seems that the -- these regiments had attached to them artillery batteries and the like, in other words, the same type of armaments that we have seen subordinated within the brigades. Is the effect of what you are saying that the corps command had at its disposal similar artillery which it could immediately command rather than through the brigades?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The idea of the corps supporting arms is that they are able to be used to directly support the corps itself, that is, the brigades that were fighting on the ground could be supported directly by the corps supporting arms, such as artillery, engineers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, more specifically, how would that chain of command work, starting from the position of the corps commander, General Galic? What are the steps from him to the corps artillery?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he wished to write an order, and in fact we have been provided with several orders relating to operations, then a set of orders would be given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I have two observations to make. First of all, this issue seems to me to be that this is a leading question that should not be admitted, but the answer was given already. And then the second issue, the question that we are talking about now, I believe that it brings confusion because we are talking about the artillery corps, but without much precision. Are we talking about artillery which was attached to a brigade? Are we talking about the artillery which is subordinated to what we can see now? I believe that things are still unclear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is there anything in particular that you would like to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, it is not a leading question. And secondly, the witness has already clearly explained that we are now talking about corps artillery, that is, artillery attached directly to the corps command rather than indirectly through the brigade structure. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is denied. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Philipps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps supporting arms are --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps if I could interrupt you. You said that you saw a set of orders. Where did those orders come from? In other words, how did you obtain them, ultimately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders themselves were part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps documents provided by the Defence and relates to orders and instructions to the brigades within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and also to the corps supporting arms. So, for example, a document will talk about -- will talk and give orders to specific brigades, as well as to specific regiments that are directly subordinated to the corps headquarters. And those are the -- those units that are directly subordinate to the corps headquarters are listed along the bottom of the chart.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue. I think you were taking us to slide 64, which is the first of those regiments attached directly to the corps command, that is, the corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The slide number 64 shows the 4th Mixed Anti-tank Artillery Regiment. This regiment consisted of a number of subunits. I have identified three artillery batteries that were part of the 4th Mixed Anti-tank Artillery Regiment. It may have had more artillery units as part of it. But I have identified three. As such, they are referred to as artillery batteries. I do not have information as to the number of Howitzers within each battery, but I would expect a minimum of four, and possibly more, in each battery.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Given what you said earlier to the effect that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I notice that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really apologise, but I believe that the rhythm does not allow for perfect interpretation. I believe that a whole half sentence escaped the attention of the French booth. And also I believe, as I'm following also the B/C/S booth, perhaps if we can slow down. I believe that the French booth just interpreted the 4th Battalion and I think what was not translated was that this was anti-tank unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it then you will slow down a bit, Mr. Ierace, and that we now understand that Mr. Piletta-Zanin has added something to the translation. Please proceed. I will follow the French booth from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have explained where the brigades were located geographically. Given the nature of these regiments, do you have any information as to whether they were in fixed permanent positions or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we do not have the interpretation, General Galic and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any specific reason why B/C/S translation is not there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It seems to be a technical problem, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any specific technical problem? Yes. I do understand that it has been restored. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will repeat the question: Were these regiments in permanent geographic positions or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any information as to the exact location of this unit or whether it moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: By this unit, do you mean this regiment or do you mean the corps artillery, generally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific information about locations of corps artillery except that battery that was detached to the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please continue, Mr. Philipps.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slide number 65 shows the 4th Mixed Artillery Regiment. In this case, I've shown one artillery battery with artillery of two different calibres: one rocket battery and a further artillery battery which was detached to the Rogatica Brigade sometime on the 23rd of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take it the Rogatica brigade was outside the Sarajevo theatre. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it did not form part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have a question mark after "rocket battery." Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really apologise. Everything is extremely technical here. I am trying to follow. I am just going to give you one example to show you the rapidity. The booth did not interpret two different calibres. They were speaking about other calibres, different calibres, and now it is two different calibres. This is only due to the rhythm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, and perhaps Mr. Philipps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What is the significance of the question mark after "rocket battery" and after the reference to the 130 millimetre M-46?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question mark after the word "rocket battery," I myself have used the term "rocket battery" and hence I have put the question mark. I had information from a document which showed a unit, a battery-sized unit, containing 128-millimetre Organj type of equipment which I have interpreted and is, in fact, a rocket. And so I have termed it a "rocket battery," and hence the question mark. The term "rocket battery," I believe is not used in the document itself. The question mark after the 130 millimetre M-46, the M-46 is what I have interpreted as being the type of weapon used. The only, as I understand, the 130 millimetre was given in the document, but the actual type of weapon, the M-46, is something that I have included through analysis and therefore have put in the question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the right of this diagram is also shown a T-12, and this is a type of anti-tank weapon with a calibre of 100 millimetres. Slide number 66 of the corps supporting arms shows the 4th Light Anti-aircraft Artillery Regiment. I have shown only one battery as being part of this regiment, as I only have information on that one battery. There may have been more batteries and, indeed, within a regiment one would expect several more batteries. The battery shown is divided into two parts, two light anti-aircraft platoons with a variety of anti-aircraft cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just in relation to the anti-aircraft cannons, do you know whether the larger calibres were independently mobile or on a trailer or in some other form, and in particular, what mobility they had?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within where it is shown the 2nd Light Anti-aircraft Platoon, these guns were of varying mobility. Some were relatively small and had wheels and could be manhandled or towed, and some were relatively large, such as the 40 millimetre anti-aircraft gun, and would have to be moved by towing, but was not self-propelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before you move on, we have heard evidence of the existence of APCs which had guns mounted on them. Whereabouts did APCs fit in to this chart? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw previously in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade that there was an armoured battalion. And within that armoured battalion, there were T-55 tanks and mechanised infantry combat vehicles, sometimes called APCs or armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you briefly explain to us the essential difference between an armoured battalion and a mechanised battalion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, an armoured battalion would consist mostly of tanks with a few mechanised infantry combat vehicles, whereas a mechanised battalion mostly consists of mechanised armoured vehicles, not tanks. It is to do with the ratio generally and the type of equipment between the two organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And, again, what is an example of a mechanised armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one that we see or that we have a document relating to is actually called a Praga, P-r-a-g-a. And this vehicle is armed with a 20-millimetre cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slide number 67 shows the 4th Military Police Battalion directly subordinated to the corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, just stopping there for a moment. On slide 67, you are saying, I take it, that you have seen documentary evidence from more than one source, given the firmness of the line, that there was a military police battalion attached directly to the corps headquarters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the interpretation, Your Honour. I didn't even hear the question of my learned colleague. I didn't hear it and General Galic didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am happy to repeat it for the benefit of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question was: "Now, just stopping there for a moment. On slide 67, you are saying, I take it, that you have seen documentary evidence from more than one source, given the firmness of the line, that there was a military police battalion attached directly to the corps headquarters. Is that correct?" Answer: "That's correct." Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slide number 68 shows the 4th Communications Battalion that was responsible for the communications within the corps headquarters and from the corps headquarters to the brigades. Slide number 69 shows the headquarters of the 4th Engineer Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise. In relation to the communications battalion attached to the corps headquarters, did the documents give you any insight as to the nature of their responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically without me speculating, which would not be of value.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slide number 69 shows the 4th Engineer Battalion. The units subordinated to this battalion are shown probably in part, and here they consist of an obstacle construction group, a mobile obstacle construction group, and a group for road maintenance. There would probably be other squadrons or companies that formed part of this battalion, but I have no information on those. Slide number 70 shows the 4th Transport Battalion, responsible for providing transport in the form of trucks to the corps headquarters and in assistance to supplying the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is the reference to Lukavica a reference to their location?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 4th Transport Battalion was located in the forward command post at Lukavica, but most of the transport battalion itself would have been located elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You just referred to Lukavica as the forward command post --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am trying to follow what is going on in the B/C/S booth, and I believe that it is still going very fast. I have the impression that the last thing was not interpreted because things are going very quickly. I just wanted to let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please keep in mind the speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You referred to Lukavica as the forward command post. What do you understand by "forward command post," and was that a reference in the documentation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perhaps should have been more specific. When referring to Lukavica, I am referring to the corps forward command post which was in that location and co-located with other parts of the corps, such as some of the staff officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were there references to Lukavica as being the corps forward command post in the documentation that you received from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there are multiple references to Lukavica as the corps forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The terminology "forward command post" perhaps suggests that there was a more central command post. Is that understanding of the language correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the way that the question has been asked seems to make it a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if this is really an issue. But in any event, the first part was not leading. I will rephrase the second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you see any documentation which emanated from the Defence which cast any light on whether there was a more central command post?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, a corps headquarters or the corps headquarters in question would have several command posts, a forward command post at Lukavica, and really the main headquarters where most of the logistics work would be done, and that, I believe, was in Pale, though I would have to check the document. And the forward command post itself was capable of moving with the corps commander to wherever he chose to move it, whereas the main corps headquarters would generally stay within the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you see any references in the documentation from the Defence to any other forward command posts for the SRK?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check the documents again. But I believe at one time the forward command post was moved to a position north of Sarajevo or elsewhere. This may have occurred, but I would have to check the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slide number 71 shows the 4th Medical Battalion. Information underneath also shows there was a Sarajevo military medical centre which also was responsible for the medical services for the corps. Slide number 72 shows the 4th Reconnaissance Company. This organisation would be responsible for specific reconnaissance tasks directed by the corps headquarters. Slide number 73 shows an atomic, biological and chemical defence company sometimes termed "NBC Defence Company" or in B/C/S, that would be ABHO. The function of this company was biological and chemical defence, that is, issuing warning and notices of any use by the enemy of any of these means. And that is the concluding slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. On the chart to the right of the box which encapsules the corps operational staff, there appear two small boxes. The first and closest is titled "Pretis factory." Could you explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included this box on the chart as the Pretis factory was the main supplier of shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know where that was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pretis factory was to the north of Sarajevo, in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please point out that box on the chart.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you also now explain the box which appears to its right, and for the record, that reads as follows: Novo Sarajevo Chetnik detachment - November 1993 - July 1995, there under a green forefigure as opposed to a head and shoulders. Underneath that, capitals Alexic and capitals Slavko. Underneath that, " - November 1993 - ." Underneath that, dot commander.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of the chart represents a unit which is not or does not appear to be subordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, but which operated within the corps area. There is no documentation that quotes a "VP" number or vojni post number for this organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When you say that it does not appear to be subordinated, do you refer to the documents or material other than the documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is referring to all documentation that I have consulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And what was the source of information for the dates which appear in the box?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to check and look up the index to the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the source of information for the title of the box?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this would be a direct translation from one of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do I take it, therefore, that there was a document, indeed, it would seem a document which referred to the unit in those terms and referred to those dates?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would have to check precisely which document or indeed statement refers to this box.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that source indicated in the document attached to your statement, that is, the approximately 60-page document listing the sources?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be in that alphabetically under the list both of units and of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the corps as a whole, by examining the documents, did you discern chains or lines of communication, firstly, in a downwards direction, that is, from the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lines on the diagram represent chains of command as well as chains of communication. The reason I say that is, quite clearly, brigade commanders would communicate with each other, but I have not shown those lines on the diagram. I have only shown those lines relating to direct command of units and of subunits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you refer to lines of communication in both directions when you say that, or one direction? In other words, up and down the chain of command or just down?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These lines represent a chain of command, and by definition, a chain of command provides orders in one direction and receives information and intelligence in the other direction. So the lines represent a flow of information as well as command between the formations units and subunits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have referred in your explanation to infantry brigades, mechanised brigades, and light infantry brigades. Could you please explain the essential difference or differences between them.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, this relates to the equipment and to, in the case of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the number of troops within an organisation. The infantry brigades are generally slightly stronger, and in some cases, much stronger than the light infantry brigades. There may be also differences in equipment such as artillery and other supporting arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And in relation to the mechanised brigades, is that similar to your explanation for the mechanised battalions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very similar. The main difference between, in this case, a mechanised brigade and an infantry brigade is that the mechanised brigade would actually have one mechanised battalion attached to it. Because it is termed a "mechanised brigade" in this case does not mean that the entire brigade was capable of moving in armoured or mechanised equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are open session again. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Philipps, good afternoon. Mr. Philipps, bearing in mind that we have your diagram in front of us, we would like to ask you first a question in relation to the information that you have about the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, Mr. Tomislav Sipcic. You said that you put it on your chart that Mr. Sipcic, it says here July 1992, August 1992. Could you perhaps clarify this for us. What do you mean by putting here "July 1992"? Is that when Mr. Sipcic was appointed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That date has a dash in front of it, as I remember, and represents the date when I have knowledge or a document that shows General Sipcic in that position. And the last piece of information I have about him is shown on the second date. They do not show the dates that he took over or that he relinquished his position, but show information where on those dates he was or I have information that he was the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one thing: Whenever it would be possible to put the relevant chart on our screens, that would highly facilitate the understanding of the expertise. We don't have to repeat it for now, but perhaps for the next questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Philipps, July or August, which -- what is the date of the document on the basis of which you claim that Mr. Sipcic was the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look up on the index the specific ERN number for the document or for the statement that refers to General Sipcic as being in that position on those dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us about the document on the basis of which you had this information? Could you tell us about the source of the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I would have to look it up to know which document I had used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just ask you: The documents are not accessible by your computer or are they stored in the computer? Is it something you could immediately do or otherwise perhaps you make a list, what you could perhaps do during the next break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can look up the document reference number straight away and describe what the document or statement was, and I can do that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it then we get something like in your annex or is there more information contained in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just simply my list showing a brief description of the document or witness statement and the date it was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is easily done, please do it whenever you have to consult one of the documents. I don't know whether you can do it for Mr. Sipcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I consult the list on my left here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the list attached to your -- yes, that is part of your report so you may consult that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first reference I have provides an ERN number and then refers to the appointment of Major Marko Zubic, a major in the reserve to the logistic staff of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. The second reference refers to a witness statement given by Colonel Aleksa Krsmanovic, and again I can provide the ERNs if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Philipps, for the ERN number regarding Aleksa Krsmanovic. But I'm interested about the first document. You said that this was appointment of Mr. Marko Zubic, who was then appointed. On that first document that you were able to use, do you have the signature of Mr. Sipcic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I would have to refer to the document itself. When compiling this chart, I used almost -- well, read over 2500 documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us the date of the appointment in this document whereby Marko Zubic is appointed general?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I would have to refer to the document itself, not having memorised the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps tell us the source of this document that you were able to have at your disposal and to use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PHILIPPS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I am afraid I would have to look at the document itself to find the source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, in order to short-cut this way of questioning, I see that the documents concerned are mentioned in the list, the alphabetical list of persons attached to the witness statement. It is almost not imaginable that the witness would know by heart all of these documents. You know, apparently, what the document is about. So in order to save time, I would say that you confront then the witness with the document if you want to know more about the document but not ask six, seven, eight questions about the document of which apparently the witness has no -- nothing in his memory at this moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must stress the Defence was not able to have a look at this document, no matter how hard we tried and tried to find certain documents according to the ERN numbers. Unfortunately, for technical reasons, this was not possible. And particularly would like to stress that when we are talking about the documents that were disclosed to the Prosecution by the Defence, the ERN number for the Defence has no meaning. It is not much of an information. It is not likely the Defence would be able to locate this document. So the list of the documents of the Defence that the Prosecution received is determined by dates and other numbers. Yesterday I told my learned colleague that we would like to have dates for documents. But at the moment I would just like to stress, the Defence was never able to have a look at this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it take you to retrieve that document, Mr. Philipps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be possible to retrieve it either from our system within a relatively short period of time, half an hour, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since we are just talking about the retrieval of documents, would there be a way of making a request to retrieve documents, Mr. Ierace, while Mr. Philipps is questioned? Of course, starting from the assumption that the Defence has had no opportunity to see the document, but perhaps you would first comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes. You may remember that, in May, I raised this issue whether you required the Prosecution to file a copy of all of these documents since they are already either been disclosed to the Defence or they have come from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I mean before May. Might I suggest, Mr. President, there may be a hard copy set that the witness could refer to. Perhaps, through you, I could enquire of the witness as to whether there is a hard copy set in existence, one set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that be a hard copy set with the following order of the ERN numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would mean that if the hard copy set would be here --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Then the witness could immediately locate the document. I am not sure there is, but perhaps the witness could be asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
